headline: Flight to quality is the dominant demand driver: occupiers are competing for scarce sustainable Grade A space, AI firms are a new source of demand, and secondary stock faces an ESG cliff.
summary: Carter Jonas notes that demand for high-quality, sustainable Grade A space continues to outstrip supply, particularly in the West End, Midtown and the City. That matches Grade A vacancy of only 1.9% (1.3% in the West End and City, Avison Young). AI companies took about 700,000 sq ft in H1 2026 (Avison Young) and favour large, highly specified, well-connected buildings. On ESG, the government's proposed MEES trajectory (EPC C by 2027, EPC B by 2030 for commercial lettings) remains the key regulatory risk for older stock; the final timetable should be confirmed before any decisions are made.
insights: Flight to quality: demand for sustainable Grade A space is outstripping supply in the West End, Midtown and City (Carter Jonas Q2 2026).
AI occupiers (Anthropic, OpenAI and others) prioritise high-spec, amenity-rich buildings in the West End and King's Cross.
Refurbishment-led supply (about two-thirds of 2025 starts) reflects both cost and embodied-carbon policy, i.e. 'retrofit first'.
ESG: proposed MEES minimum of EPC C (2027) and B (2030) for lettings. Assets rated D-G face capex or obsolescence; confirm the latest government position.

signals.title: Retrofit-to-prime strategy
signals.rationale: Buying well-located secondary buildings and upgrading them to EPC A/B Grade A meets unmet demand at a lower carbon and cost basis than new build.

signals.title: ESG stranding of secondary stock
signals.rationale: Buildings unable to reach the MEES trajectory face letting restrictions, higher capex and value discounts.
